'''Laurence Chisholm Young''' (14 July 1905 – 24 December 2000) was a British [[mathematician]] known for his contributions to [[measure theory]], the [[calculus of variations]], [[optimal control theory]], and [[potential theory]].  He was the son of [[William Henry Young]] and [[Grace Chisholm Young]], both prominent mathematicians. He moved to the US in 1949 but never sought American citizenship.

The concept of [[Young measure]] is named after him: he also introduced the concept of the [[generalized curve]]<ref>{{harv|Young|1937}}.</ref> and a concept of generalized surface<ref>{{harv|Young|1951}}.</ref> which later evolved in the concept of [[varifold]].<ref>In his commemorative papers describing the research of Almgren, {{harvs|txt|first1=Brian|last1=White|author1-link= Brian White (mathematician)|year=1997|year2=1998|loc1=p.1452, footnote 1|loc2=p.682, footnote 1}} writes that these are "''essentially the same class of surfaces''". He notes also that Young himself used the same term in a somewhat different context i.e. in {{harvs|first=L. C.|last=Young|year1=1942|year2=1942a}}.</ref><ref>See also the [https://www.dam.brown.edu/people/documents/Geometic_000.pdf 2015 unpublished essay] of his pupil [[Wendell Fleming]].</ref> The Young integral also is named after him and has now been generalised in the theory of [[rough paths]].<ref>{{harv|Young|1936}}.</ref>

==Life and academic career==
Laurence Chisholm Young was born in [[Göttingen]],<ref name="mr2001">{{harv|Turner|Rabinowitz|Rudin|2001}}.</ref> the fifth of the six children of [[William Henry Young]] and [[Grace Chisholm Young]].<ref name="FW413" >{{harv|Fleming|Wiegand|2004|p=413}}.</ref> He held positions of Professor at the University of Cape Town, South Africa, and at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. He was also a chess grandmaster.<ref>[https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/young.htm Grace Chisholm Young at Biographies of Women Mathematicians]</ref>
